name: Discrete Maths for Programmers
description: The maths under programming: logic, sets and functions, counting, logarithms, modular arithmetic, probability, proofs and invariants, graph theory and computability.

modules.name: Logic, Sets & Counting
modules.description: Boolean logic and De Morgan's laws, sets and functions, permutations and combinations, logarithms, pigeonhole and modular arithmetic.

cards.code:
from itertools import product
cases = list(product([True, False], repeat=2))
print(all((not (a and b)) == ((not a) or (not b)) for a, b in cases))
print(all((not (a or b)) == ((not a) and (not b)) for a, b in cases))
cards.explanation: De Morgan's laws: `not (a and b)` equals `(not a) or (not b)`, and `not (a or b)` equals `(not a) and (not b)`. Checking every combination of inputs — a truth table — proves it. They are the everyday tool for simplifying and correctly negating conditions, such as turning "keep if valid and active" into "skip if invalid or inactive".

cards.prompt: What are injective, surjective and bijective functions, and why do programmers care?
cards.answer: Injective (one-to-one): different inputs never map to the same output. Surjective (onto): every possible output is produced by some input. Bijective: both — a perfect pairing, so the function has an inverse.
cards.explanation: An encoding must be injective to be decodable (base64, UTF-8); a hash function from long strings to 64 bits cannot be, so collisions must exist. Lossless round trips (`decode(encode(x)) == x`) need a bijection on the values you care about — a property worth testing directly.

Permutations count ordered selections — P(5,2) = 5 × 4 = 20. Combinations count unordered ones — C(5,2) = 20 / 2! = 10. A set of n items has 2ⁿ subsets (each item is in or out), and n items can be ordered in n! ways. These formulas estimate brute-force search spaces, test-case counts and password strength.

cards.prompt: Why does O(log n) appear so often, and why is the base of the logarithm irrelevant in Big O?
cards.answer: log₂ n is the number of times you can halve n before reaching 1 — so any algorithm that discards half the remaining work each step (binary search, balanced trees, divide and conquer) takes about log n steps. Logarithms in different bases differ only by a constant factor (log₂ n = log₁₀ n / log₁₀ 2), which Big O ignores.
cards.explanation: Intuition: log₂ of a thousand is about 10, of a million about 20, of a billion about 30. Doubling the input adds just one step — which is why O(log n) operations feel constant in practice.

cards.prompt: What is the pigeonhole principle, and what does it prove in computing?
cards.answer: If n items are placed into m boxes with n > m, at least one box holds more than one item. So any hash from arbitrary inputs to a fixed-size output must have collisions, and no lossless compression scheme can shrink every possible file.
cards.explanation: It turns "surely this is unique enough" into a counting argument. Collisions cannot be prevented, only made improbable (large outputs) or handled (hash tables compare keys after matching hashes).

cards.prompt: In Python, what does this print?
cards.explanation: Modular arithmetic works with remainders — clock arithmetic. Python's `%` takes the sign of the divisor, so `-7 % 3` is 2 (C and Java give -1). `pow(base, exp, mod)` computes huge modular powers efficiently by repeated squaring, the core operation of RSA and Diffie–Hellman. `(a * b) % m` equals `((a % m) * (b % m)) % m`, which keeps hash computations bounded.

modules.name: Probability, Proofs & Computability
modules.description: Probability and expectation, the birthday paradox, Bayes and base rates, induction and invariants, graph theory and undecidability.

cards.prompt: What are independence, conditional probability and expected value?
cards.answer: Independent events do not affect each other, so P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Conditional probability P(A | B) is the chance of A given that B happened. Expected value is the probability-weighted average outcome — the long-run mean.
cards.explanation: Engineering uses them constantly: if each of 20 independent services is up 99.9% of the time, all are up only about 98% (0.999²⁰); a retry succeeds if any attempt does; expected cost drives decisions like whether to cache. The classic mistake is assuming independence between failures that share a cause — the same region, deploy or dependency.

cards.prompt: What does this print — the chance that at least two of 23 people share a birthday, and of a collision among 1 million random 64-bit IDs?
cards.explanation: The probability of no collision among k items drawn from n possibilities is the product of (1 − i/n); 23 people already give over 50%. Collisions become likely around √n draws — the birthday bound. For 64-bit IDs that is about 4 billion, and a million IDs is still safe; 32-bit IDs would collide after roughly 77,000.

cards.prompt: A fraud detector catches 99% of fraud and wrongly flags only 1% of legitimate transactions. Fraud is 1 in 1,000 transactions. If a transaction is flagged, how likely is it to be fraud?
cards.answer: About 9%. Out of 100,000 transactions, 100 are fraud and 99 of them are flagged; of the 99,900 legitimate ones, 1% — about 999 — are also flagged. So only 99 of roughly 1,098 flags are real fraud.
cards.explanation: This is Bayes' theorem and the base-rate fallacy: when the thing you are looking for is rare, even an accurate test produces mostly false positives. It governs alerting, security scanners, medical tests and ML classifiers — always ask about the base rate before trusting a flag.

cards.prompt: What is proof by induction, and how do loop invariants use the same idea?
cards.answer: Induction proves a statement for all n by proving it for a base case and then showing that if it holds for n, it holds for n + 1. A loop invariant is a condition true before the loop and preserved by every iteration; combined with the exit condition it proves the loop's result correct.
cards.explanation: For binary search, the invariant "if the target exists, it is within [low, high]" is exactly what makes the boundary updates correct, and what off-by-one bugs violate. Stating the invariant as a comment or assertion is the cheapest way to get tricky loops right.

cards.prompt: What are the core graph-theory terms every programmer should know?
cards.answer: Vertices (nodes) and edges; directed versus undirected; weighted edges; degree (number of edges at a node); paths and cycles; connected components; trees (connected and acyclic, with exactly n − 1 edges); DAGs (directed acyclic graphs); and bipartite graphs (two groups with edges only between them).
cards.explanation: Recognising the graph in a problem is most of the work: dependencies are a DAG (topological sort), networks are weighted graphs (shortest paths), matching problems are bipartite, and social networks raise connectivity questions. The algorithms then follow from the shape.

cards.prompt: What is the halting problem, and what does it mean for tools that analyse code?
cards.answer: Turing proved no program can decide, for every program and input, whether it eventually halts. Rice's theorem generalises this: any non-trivial question about a program's behaviour — "does it ever dereference null?", "is this code reachable?" — is undecidable in general.
cards.explanation: That is why every static analyser, type checker and linter must approximate: it either rejects some correct programs (conservative — type systems) or misses some bugs (heuristic — linters), and why perfect automatic bug detection is impossible, not merely unsolved.
